messages.subject: collostructional analysis
messages.body_plain:
I am learning to use coll.analysis, specifically simple collexeme
analysis. I want to investigate preference of certain lexemes to a
certain slot of a construction.

So, basically, I do the following:

I detect all cases of the construction I want to investigate
(totalling round 200 cases in the whole BNC);
I build up a table with all the cases (w1, ¬w1, c, ¬c);
I save it as tab-separated file;
I run coll.analysis giving thar file as input and, finally;
I obtain the file containing the attraction/repelled list of
collexemes ranked according to Fisher-Yates.

But I have a question as how to report the results given by the
association measure:

 I have seen in the case studies in Stefanowitsch and Gries (2003,
others) that they use the exponential notation (e.g tell 1.6E-127;
wish 3.11E-06; send 7.26E-68 , etc.) to report results. What I don't
know is how to get from the scores that coll.analysis gives, such as
"tell (3206.235037)" or "send (303.517837)" (fairly high scores) to
that exponential notation (very small numbers). I get lost in the part
concerning the negative log transformation.

Could you please give some easy step-by-step explanation and examples
how to do this and how to manage those in R?

Thank you and sorry if the question wasn't interesting enough or
incosistent

messages.subject: Re: [StatForLing with R] collostructional analysis
messages.body_plain:
Hi

> I build up a table with all the cases (w1, ¬w1, c, ¬c);
> I save it as tab-separated file;
> I run coll.analysis giving thar file as input and, finally;

Hm, I hope you do this right because this kind of 4-column table is
not the typical type of input (cf. the readme at
<http://tinyurl.com/collostructions>) ...

As for the logging: the large values are -log10 of the small values.
That is, in the case of tell (from Stefanowitsch and Gries 2003:229),
the value in the table is 1.6E-127, which in later studies would be
reported as

> -log10(1.6E-127)
[1] 126.7959 # this value!

And this would be the reverse:

> 10^-126.7959
[1] 1.599926e-127 # cf. above

HTH,
STG
--
Stefan Th. Gries
-----------------------------------------------
University of California, Santa Barbara
http://www.linguistics.ucsb.edu/faculty/stgries
-----------------------------------------------

Thank you for you answer, Stefan:

Sorry, saying "w1, ¬w1, c, ¬c" was confusing/wrong. What I meant was
that I entered a table like the following as input to R:

WORD	FREQ_WORD_in_CORPUS	FREQ_WORD_in_DITRANSITIVE
word a
word b
word c
...

On the other hand, I will practise the logging as you explained it.

Finally, my last question (I promise!) is whether, after the simple
collexeme analysis, it would be possible to run a cluster analysis
considering that the structure under study is not very frequent in the
BNC (again, round 200) or whether this clustering is only reserved to
large quantities of examples or larger corpora.

Best!

messages.subject: Re: collostructional analysis
messages.body_plain:
Basically, in the example I'm practising with, I have seen that in my
list of nouns attracted to some verbs, only generic nouns (e.g
"People") appear when these verbs realize the predicate, whereas more
specific or personal pronouns are repelled as subjects (e.g "John").
So I wished to explore whether cluster analysis will group these nouns
according to generic vs specific, and whether it could, more
importantly, suggest further semantic subgroups.

In the example with verbs that you give, I guess that cluster analysis
would suggest, say, whether verbs strongly attracted to the
ditransitive structure can be grouped according to "verbs of speech"
or "verbs expressing movement", etc.

I don't know if I'm on the right track, just beginning with all this,
sorry.

Thank for all the feedback and wouldn't like to take much more of your
time.
